reason: The era sense is consistently 'age' in the run, including where tradition has 'world' (Matt 13:22, Mark 4:19, Rom 12:2, 2 Cor 4:4), but two things vary by chapter. The doxology formula εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων is 'forever and ever' in 2 Timothy, 1 Peter and Revelation but 'to the ages of the ages' in Gal 1:5, Phil 4:20 and 1 Tim 1:17, with 'the age of the ages' at Eph 3:21. The created-order sense is 'the ages' at Heb 1:2 but 'the worlds' at Heb 11:3. An entry is needed to fix 'age' for the era sense and settle the idioms.
sense: a period of time, an era; especially the present age contrasted with the age to come, and the plural 'ages' as spans of history

alternates.when: The idiom εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα or εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας in a positive statement (e.g. John 6:51, Rom 11:36, Heb 5:6, Heb 13:8, Jude 13).
The idiom εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα with a negative, meaning 'not ever' (e.g. Matt 21:19, Mark 3:29, John 4:14, John 8:51, John 13:8, 1 Cor 8:13).

The doubled formula εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος or εἰς αἰῶνας αἰώνων, in every book (Gal 1:5, Phil 4:20, 1 Tim 1:17, 2 Tim 4:18, Heb 1:8, 1 Peter, Revelation). At Eph 3:21 render the closing phrase 'to all generations, forever and ever'. Do not use 'to the ages of the ages'; a footnote may give the literal form where a wordplay with 'age' is nearby.
The idioms ἀπ' αἰῶνος (Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21, Acts 15:18) and ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος (John 9:32), meaning from the distant past or since the beginning of time.
The plural as object of making or ordering, meaning the whole created order (Heb 1:2, Heb 11:3 only). Prefer 'universe' in both verses so they match; a note may say the Greek is literally 'the ages'.
The unique phrase εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος at 2 Pet 3:18, rendered 'to the day of eternity'.

traditional: world for the era sense in many verses (KJV 'this world', 'the end of the world', 'the god of this world'), age in others; for ever and for ever and ever in the idioms
rationale: The word is a time-word. Where it stands alone it means an era, and New Testament writers share the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come; 'world' blurs this and confuses it with a different Greek word (kosmos) that really does mean 'world'. In the fixed phrases 'into the age' and 'into the ages of the ages' a first-century reader simply heard 'forever' or, with a negative, 'never', so those are translated as the idioms they are. A word-for-word 'to the ages of the ages' sounds exotic in English where the Greek sounded ordinary.
standard_view: Standard lexicons give the same senses: a long time or eternity in the idioms, a segment of time or age, and the world as a created order in Heb 1:2 and 11:3. Modern translations (ESV, NRSV, NIV, CSB) use 'age' in 'end of the age', 'this age' and 'the age to come', but several keep 'world' at places like Matt 13:22, Mark 4:19, Rom 12:2 and 2 Cor 4:4; the default here uses 'age' there too, which lexicographers accept and some versions (CSB, NET in places) already do. Nearly all render the doubled formula 'forever and ever'; a few literal versions (Young's, and Orthodox liturgical English, 'unto the ages of ages') keep the word-for-word form. At Eph 3:11 and 1 Tim 1:17 many versions paraphrase as 'eternal purpose' and 'King eternal'; 'purpose of the ages' and 'King of the ages' follow the default and are also widely used.
